examples.problem_statement: Derive the general formula for the standard quadratic equation $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ using the Pūraṇa method.

solution.description: Begin from the general quadratic written in standard form, with a not equal to zero so that the equation really is of the second degree.
Divide every term by a so the leading coefficient becomes 1. Completing the square needs a bare x squared term, which is what this normalising step provides.
Move the constant term c over a to the right-hand side, leaving only the x squared and x terms on the left. Those two terms are the ones that will be completed into a square.

Add the square of half the coefficient of x, that is b over 2a all squared, to both sides. Adding it on both sides keeps the equation balanced while turning the left side into a perfect square; this is the Purana or completion step itself.
Rewrite the left side in its closed form as x plus b over 2a, all squared, and leave the two constant terms standing on the right.
Put the right-hand side over the common denominator 4a squared. The two terms collect into b squared minus 4ac over 4a squared, so the discriminant appears on its own.

solution.operation: Take square root of both sides
solution.description: Take the square root of both sides. A square has two roots, so the right side acquires a plus-or-minus sign, and that sign is where the two solutions come from.
Subtract b over 2a from both sides to leave x by itself on the left.
Both terms on the right already share the denominator 2a, so combine them into a single fraction. What remains is the quadratic formula in its usual shape.

concept.technique_name: completing the cube with a shift substitution

solution.description: Start from the cubic exactly as given, with all four terms on the left. The plan is to recast the left side so that a perfect cube appears in place of the loose terms.
Transpose the linear and constant terms to the right, keeping x cubed and minus 6x squared together on the left, because those two are how the cube of a binomial begins.
Write out the expansion of x minus 2, all cubed, for comparison. It opens with the same x cubed minus 6x squared and differs only in the 12x and the minus 8 that follow.
Supply that missing 12x minus 8 on both sides. The left becomes exactly x minus 2, all cubed, while the right, using the transposed form from step 2, collapses to just x minus 2.
Set y equal to x minus 2. The equation then reads y cubed equals y, which is far easier to handle than the original cubic.
Bring both terms to one side and factor: y times y minus 1 times y plus 1 equals zero.
By the zero product rule each factor supplies a root, so y is 0, 1 or minus 1.
Undo the substitution. Since y was defined as x minus 2, every root in y becomes an x by adding 2 back.
Adding 2 to each of 0, 1 and minus 1 gives the three roots of the original cubic: x equals 2, 3 and 1.
Transpose the linear and constant terms of this cubic to the right, leaving x cubed and 6x squared on the left. It is the same opening move as before, with the signs now all positive.
Compare with x plus 2, all cubed, whose expansion carries an extra 12x plus 8. Supplying those to both sides makes the left a perfect cube and reduces the right to x plus 2.
Write y for x plus 2, which turns the equation into y cubed equals y, the same simple form reached in the first example.
Read the roots 0, 1 and minus 1 off y cubed equals y, then subtract 2 from each to return to x, giving minus 2, minus 1 and minus 3.
Transpose the linear and constant terms so that x cubed and 6x squared stand alone on the left, ready to be completed into a cube.
Completing x plus 2, all cubed, adds 12x plus 8 to both sides. The right side becomes 49x minus 22, which rewritten around x plus 2 is 49 times x plus 2, less 120.

With y standing for x plus 2 the equation becomes y cubed minus 49y plus 120 equals zero. Here the cube does not reduce to y cubed equals y, so the new cubic in y must be factored; y minus 3 comes out, leaving y squared plus 3y minus 40.
Factor that quadratic as y minus 5 times y plus 8, so the three roots in y are 3, 5 and minus 8.
Return to x by subtracting 2 from each root in y, which gives x equal to 1, 3 and minus 10.
